hook: Pair a baby girl with a toy screwdriver or fire truck, and the AI fortune-teller still sees a nurse or a fashion model in her future.
lede: In the Chinese zhuazhou ritual, the object a baby picks is read as a sign of the life to come. Cradle of Success hands that ritual to generative AI. Visitors choose a baby photograph and a toy, and the machine answers with a fortune printed like a temple slip and a video of a whole life, from age 1 to 100. The futures it foretells are rarely unforeseen. They are society’s stereotypes, delivered with the authority of prophecy.

chapters.title: Pick a baby, pick a toy
paragraphs: Under low light, a wooden cradle holds children’s toys, found by searching for “Zhuazhou objects” on online shopping platforms, and an album of AI-generated baby portraits. Visitors choose a baby and set its photo in an NFC-enabled frame, then choose a toy and place it on a platform beside it, indicating a potential career for that child.

A printer releases a paper fortune, and screens above a Shinto-style plank play the baby’s predicted life. The last move belongs to the visitor. Anyone who feels they have drawn a bad fortune can tie the slip to the plank, as people do with an unfavorable omikuji at a Japanese shrine.

figures.caption: The cradle and its toys, beneath rows of screens playing AI-generated lives.

The visit in four steps: select a baby photo, choose an object from the cradle, receive a printed fortune and a video of the predicted life, and post the slip on the plank if it feels like bad fortune.

chapters.title: Fortunes built from stereotypes, on purpose
paragraphs: Each stage was made with a different model. The babies came from Tencent Yuanbao, a free text-to-image model: frontal portraits across four racial groups, with no obvious gender characteristics. We deliberately wrote stereotypical descriptions into the prompts, such as blond or light brown hair for white babies and black hair for Asian babies, and the portraits came back hyper-realistic.

DeepSeek wrote the fortunes in three steps. Following the traditional idea that “fortune and misfortune coexist”, it first drafted a life with a built-in reversal: in one, a Silicon Valley programmer develops a globally influential AI framework, only to be replaced by the optimization systems he created. It then compressed the story into a rhymed seven-character quatrain in the style of temple fortune slips, and extracted four keywords carrying a sense of ironic stereotype, each no more than two words in English.

Finally, Stable Diffusion with the Deforum plugin turned each narrative into a video of ten life stages, from age 1 to 100. The prompts were kept extremely minimal: an age, a race, and a few words about a profession. The model supplied the rest.

figures.caption: Baby portraits generated from prompts that specify race along with stereotyped hair color and texture.
From fate narrative to seven-character quatrain to keywords such as “Code Prophet” and “Self Fired”, assembled into the printed fortune paper.
Minimal age-based prompts, and the frames they produced at age 1 and at age 100.

chapters.title: The future the machine expects
paragraphs: The outputs were strikingly consistent. Generated futures often assigned medical or technical professions to Asian babies and professional athletics to African American babies. Female subjects stayed in gendered roles such as nursing or fashion, even when the chosen toy was a screwdriver or a fire truck, objects traditionally coded as masculine.

The models showed no capacity for self-examination or value judgment. To maximize relevance to a prompt, they retrieve the most statistically probable, most strongly associated features in their training data, whatever their factual accuracy or ethical implications. On topics such as destiny or race, we argue, current GenAI models function more like high-fidelity, unfiltered “bias amplifiers”.

quote.text: To GenAI, we are all part of a heteronormative male-dominated world where outliers are conveniently pigeon-holed as “societal expectations.”

figures.caption: Two generated futures at age 16: the Asian baby becomes a “technical guy”, the African baby an athlete.

chapters.title: A better start, the same ending
paragraphs: Visitors often chose babies or toys unlike their own lived experience, as if trying to resist a predetermined social trajectory. The predictions frequently failed to oblige. Even a starting point that seemed “better” could unfold into an undesirable or limiting future.

Faced with these futures, many visitors tied their slips to the plank, symbolically abandoning the bad fortune. That repeated gesture of letting go, rather than the prediction itself, became the work’s moment of reflection.

The version shown at the Hong Kong Arts Centre in February 2026 added more screens and introduced the life videos, which we expected to make predicted paths more immediate. Rendered as continuous life progressions, the embedded stereotypes also became more visible, and at times ironic. This configuration is the finalized version of the work.

figures.caption: The finalized layout: ten mini LED screens play the generated videos above the posted fortunes; a stand holds the interactive photo frame and base; the cradle holds the album and objects.

chapters.title: Surfacing the bias, not correcting it
paragraphs: Cradle of Success does not try to fix these predictions. It treats them as material: evidence of the value structures implicit in AI systems, placed inside a familiar ritual, where visitors can watch how easily hope, bias and technological authority become entangled. The work was made alongside our CSCW ’26 study of GenAI fortune-telling in China, and in the studio’s words it “shows the consequences of relying on AI as a source of spiritualized fortune telling.”
It was created by a team of four:
points: Bowen Liu: artist and technical lead
Lucy Long Ling: artist and designer
Star Sijia Liu: curator and producer

takeaways: Fortune-telling has always mirrored what we hope to see; GenAI lends that mirror the authority and opacity of technology.
Asked about destiny or race, current models return the most statistically probable stereotypes and present them as prophecy.
Ritual can turn biased output into reflection: the moment visitors let go of a fortune mattered more than the fortune itself.
